items.stem: About what was the population of England and Wales in the first census of 1801?
items.answer: About 8.9 million
items.markingKey: About 8.9 million. It had doubled to about 17.9 million by 1851.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Agricultural Revolution helped cause the Industrial Revolution.
items.answer: Higher food production fed a growing population, enclosure pushed some rural workers towards towns, and farm profits provided capital for industry.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher food production fed a growing population, enclosure pushed some rural workers towards towns, and farm profits provided capital for industry. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Chloé writes: "The Industrial Revolution happened suddenly in one year." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It was a gradual process over many decades, starting in some industries and regions from about 1760.
items.markingKey: It was a gradual process over many decades, starting in some industries and regions from about 1760. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Bridgewater Canal (1761) shows transport as a cause of industrialisation.
items.answer: Built to carry coal from the Duke of Bridgewater's mines at Worsley to Manchester, it halved the price of coal in the city. Cheaper fuel and transport made factories in Manchester more profitable and encouraged canal building.
items.markingKey: Context (Built to carry coal from the Duke of Bridgewater's mines at Worsley to Manchester, it halved the price of coal in the city.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: cheaper fuel and transport made factories in Manchester more profitable and encouraged canal building. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transport as a cause of industrialisation.

items.stem: British coal output went from 3 million tonnes in 1700 to 60 million tonnes in 1850. Which is the percentage change?
Describe the research methods you would use to answer "Why did Manchester grow so quickly between 1770 and 1850?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Collect census data (1801–1851); research the Bridgewater Canal, cotton mills and the Liverpool–Manchester Railway; read contemporary descriptions; organise causes in a diagram; evaluate sources; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect census data (1801–1851); research the Bridgewater Canal, cotton mills and the Liverpool–Manchester Railway; read contemporary descriptions; organise causes in a diagram; evaluate sources; cite in MLA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Economic treatise (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Adam Smith, "The Wealth of Nations", 1776

The author argued that dividing work into many small tasks hugely increases output. In a pin factory, ten workers each doing one or two operations could make tens of thousands of pins a day, whereas one worker doing everything might hardly make twenty.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Coal was the most important cause of the Industrial Revolution in Britain."
items.answer: Coal was essential for the later stages, but the revolution began through a combination of capital, markets, agriculture and invention.
items.markingKey: From the source: Specialisation (division of labour) greatly increases productivity. Own knowledge for: it powered steam engines and smelted iron; Britain had large, accessible deposits. Own knowledge against: without capital, markets and inventions coal would have stayed underground; early factories used water power, not coal. Judgement: Coal was essential for the later stages, but the revolution began through a combination of capital, markets, agriculture and invention. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: Aiko is investigating the causes of the Industrial Revolution in Britain and proposes the research question: "What was invented in the Industrial Revolution?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it would produce a list of inventions rather than an analysis of causes Improved: "Why did Manchester grow so quickly between 1770 and 1850?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it would produce a list of inventions rather than an analysis of causes); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "Why did Manchester grow so quickly between 1770 and 1850?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Explain why population growth encouraged industrialisation.
items.answer: More people created more demand for goods such as clothing and a larger labour force for factories and mines.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: More people created more demand for goods such as clothing and a larger labour force for factories and mines. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between domestic system and factory system.
items.answer: In the domestic system workers spun and wove at home with hand tools for a merchant; in the factory system workers came to a central building with powered machines and fixed hours.
items.markingKey: In the domestic system workers spun and wove at home with hand tools for a merchant; in the factory system workers came to a central building with powered machines and fixed hours. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Specialisation (division of labour) greatly increases productivity.
items.markingKey: Specialisation (division of labour) greatly increases productivity. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why Britain's empire and overseas trade contributed to industrialisation.
items.answer: Trade, including the profits of the slave trade and plantations, created capital and banks; colonies supplied raw cotton and bought British manufactures, creating large markets.
items.markingKey: Content: Trade, including the profits of the slave trade and plantations, created capital and banks; colonies supplied raw cotton and bought British manufactures, creating large markets. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A method of production in which workers use powered machines in a central building under supervision and fixed hours"?
items.answer: factory system
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of factory system.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "James Watt invented the steam engine." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Newcomen built a working steam engine in 1712; Watt greatly improved its efficiency and made it drive machinery.
items.markingKey: Newcomen built a working steam engine in 1712; Watt greatly improved its efficiency and made it drive machinery. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the spinning jenny and the water frame.
items.answer: The jenny was hand-powered and used at home, producing fine but weak thread; the water frame was water-powered, needed a factory and produced strong thread.
items.markingKey: The jenny was hand-powered and used at home, producing fine but weak thread; the water frame was water-powered, needed a factory and produced strong thread. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into the inventions of the Industrial Revolution and the factory system?
options: How did industry change the world?
How did the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830 affect the cost and speed of transporting cotton?
items.answer: How did the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830 affect the cost and speed of transporting cotton?
items.markingKey: B. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How did the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830 affect the cost and speed of transporting cotton?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Collect figures on canal and rail freight rates and journey times from secondary sources; read newspaper reports from 1830; record in a table; calculate % changes; evaluate reliability of figures; cite sources.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The steam engine was the most important invention of the Industrial Revolution."
items.answer: It was the most transformative single invention, but it depended on earlier inventions and resources, and spread only gradually.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it powered factories, mines, trains and ships; it freed industry from dependence on water. Arguments against: textile machines such as the water frame started the factory system; without cheap iron and coal steam engines could not be built and run. Supported judgement: It was the most transformative single invention, but it depended on earlier inventions and resources, and spread only gradually.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "factory system"?
options: A mixture of smoke and fog that pollutes the air in industrial cities
A method of production in which workers use powered machines in a central building under supervision and fixed hours
The decline of manufacturing in a region, as happened to Indian handloom weaving in the 19th century
James Watt's 1769 improvement that made steam engines far more fuel-efficient
items.answer: A method of production in which workers use powered machines in a central building under supervision and fixed hours
items.markingKey: B. "factory system" is a method of production in which workers use powered machines in a central building under supervision and fixed hours.

items.stem: Explain why inventions in spinning led to inventions in weaving.
items.answer: Faster spinning produced more thread than hand weavers could use, creating a bottleneck that encouraged inventors like Cartwright to mechanise weaving.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Faster spinning produced more thread than hand weavers could use, creating a bottleneck that encouraged inventors like Cartwright to mechanise weaving. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A – Parliamentary report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of evidence given to a Parliamentary committee on the Liverpool and Manchester Railway Bill, 1825

The engineer told the committee that a train could carry passengers between Liverpool and Manchester in under two hours, compared with about four hours by coach, and could carry heavy goods such as cotton at a lower cost than the canal.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: The railway would be faster and cheaper than coaches and canals.
items.markingKey: The railway would be faster and cheaper than coaches and canals. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: What did the 1833 Factory Act ban in textile mills?
items.answer: The employment of children under 9
items.markingKey: The employment of children under 9. Children aged 9–13 were limited to 9 hours a day.

items.stem: A student claims: "Industrial cities had high death rates because people were careless." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The causes were structural: overcrowding, no clean water, no sewers and low wages.
items.markingKey: The causes were structural: overcrowding, no clean water, no sewers and low wages. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why governments were slow to improve public health in the early 19th century.
items.answer: Many believed in laissez-faire (government should not interfere), ratepayers resisted the cost of sewers, and the miasma (bad air) theory confused the causes of disease.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many believed in laissez-faire (government should not interfere), ratepayers resisted the cost of sewers, and the miasma (bad air) theory confused the causes of disease. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Weakness: its answer is obvious and it does not focus on change, evidence or a place Improved: "How far did the 1833 Factory Act improve the lives of child workers in Lancashire cotton mills by 1847?"

items.stem:
Source A – Book on social conditions (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Friedrich Engels, "The Condition of the Working Class in England", 1845

The writer described a district of Manchester near the river where hundreds of families lived in cramped, damp cottages and cellars. There was a single privy for many people, filth lay in the courts, and the river was polluted by refuse from tanneries and dye works.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "The Industrial Revolution made life worse for most working people before 1850."
items.answer: For many workers in the short term, yes – especially in health and conditions – though historians debate living standards and conditions improved later in the century.
items.markingKey: From the source: Manchester's working-class districts were overcrowded, filthy and polluted. Own knowledge for: long hours, child labour and dangerous work in factories and mines; high death rates in overcrowded, insanitary towns. Own knowledge against: factory wages were often higher than farm wages; cheaper goods and, later, reforms improved some aspects of life. Judgement: For many workers in the short term, yes – especially in health and conditions – though historians debate living standards and conditions improved later in the century. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: Define the term "child labour".
items.answer: The employment of children in work that harms their health or education
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the employment of children in work that harms their health or education. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between government intervention and laissez-faire.
items.answer: Laissez-faire means the government leaves the economy and working conditions to employers and the market; intervention means passing laws such as Factory Acts and Public Health Acts to regulate them.
items.markingKey: Laissez-faire means the government leaves the economy and working conditions to employers and the market; intervention means passing laws such as Factory Acts and Public Health Acts to regulate them. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the Sadler Committee (1832) and explain what it reveals about working conditions and reform.
items.answer: A parliamentary committee heard evidence from child workers about 14-hour days, beatings and injuries in textile mills. Publicised testimony built pressure for the 1833 Factory Act.
items.markingKey: Context (A parliamentary committee heard evidence from child workers about 14-hour days, beatings and injuries in textile mills.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: publicised testimony built pressure for the 1833 Factory Act. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to working conditions and reform.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How far did the 1833 Factory Act improve the lives of child workers in Lancashire cotton mills by 1847?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Read the 1833 Act; read factory inspectors' reports and Sadler Committee testimony; record evidence before and after; compare with the 1847 Ten Hours Act; evaluate origin and purpose of each source; cite sources.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Read the 1833 Act; read factory inspectors' reports and Sadler Committee testimony; record evidence before and after; compare with the 1847 Ten Hours Act; evaluate origin and purpose of each source; cite sources. items.stem: Which Asian country began rapid industrialisation after the Meiji Restoration of 1868?
items.answer: Japan
items.markingKey: A. The state built railways, factories and a modern army.

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Pollution from industry was only a problem in the 20th century." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Smog, polluted rivers and disease in industrial towns were already serious in the 19th century.

Estimates by economic historians suggest that India produced about a quarter of the world's manufactured goods in 1750, but less than 2% by 1900. Over the same period Britain's share rose from under 2% to almost a fifth.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into the global impacts of industrialisation on colonies, trade and the environment, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of estimates by economic historian Paul Bairoch (1982), as cited in world-history textbooks. Purpose: to measure long-term changes in global manufacturing. Limitation: Figures for the 18th century are rough estimates built from limited data, and shares of world output do not show changes in living standards.

items.stem: Briefly explain why industrialisation is linked to climate change today.
items.answer: Since the 18th century industry has burned huge amounts of coal, then oil and gas, releasing carbon dioxide that has raised its concentration from about 280 ppm to over 420 ppm, warming the planet.

items.stem: Distinguish between a colonial economy and an industrialised economy.
items.answer: An industrialised economy produces manufactured goods with machines; a colonial economy was often shaped to export raw materials to the colonial power and import its manufactures.
items.markingKey: An industrialised economy produces manufactured goods with machines; a colonial economy was often shaped to export raw materials to the colonial power and import its manufactures. items.answer: Most British railways were built by private companies financed by investors, sometimes in a speculative "railway mania" in the 1840s.

items.answer: Local pollution affects the immediate area, such as smoky air or polluted rivers; global change, such as rising CO₂, affects the whole planet.

items.stem: Lukas argues that "The Industrial Revolution made life worse for most working people before 1850." Tomás disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: For many workers in the short term, yes – especially in health and conditions – though historians debate living standards and conditions improved later in the century.
items.markingKey: Lukas: long hours, child labour and dangerous work in factories and mines. Tomás: factory wages were often higher than farm wages. Judgement (1-2 marks): For many workers in the short term, yes – especially in health and conditions – though historians debate living standards and conditions improved later in the century.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why industrial cities suffered from air pollution.
items.answer: Burning coal in factories and homes released smoke, soot and sulphur dioxide, which combined with fog to form smog, as in London.
items.markingKey: Content: Burning coal in factories and homes released smoke, soot and sulphur dioxide, which combined with fog to form smog, as in London. items.stem:
Source A – Economic treatise (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Adam Smith, "The Wealth of Nations", 1776

The author argued that dividing work into many small tasks hugely increases output. In a pin factory, ten workers each doing one or two operations could make tens of thousands of pins a day, whereas one worker doing everything might hardly make twenty.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching the causes of the Industrial Revolution in Britain? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Adam Smith, "The Wealth of Nations", 1776. Purpose: to explain the causes of economic growth and argue for free trade and the division of labour. Value: Written as industrialisation began, it shows why contemporaries thought specialisation raised productivity. Limitation: It is a theoretical argument by an economist and does not describe workers' experiences or the role of machines.

items.stem:
Source A – Parliamentary report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of evidence given to a Parliamentary committee on the Liverpool and Manchester Railway Bill, 1825

The engineer told the committee that a train could carry passengers between Liverpool and Manchester in under two hours, compared with about four hours by coach, and could carry heavy goods such as cotton at a lower cost than the canal.

"The steam engine was the most important invention of the Industrial Revolution." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: It was the most transformative single invention, but it depended on earlier inventions and resources, and spread only gradually.
items.markingKey: From the source: The railway would be faster and cheaper than coaches and canals. Own knowledge for: it powered factories, mines, trains and ships; it freed industry from dependence on water. Own knowledge against: textile machines such as the water frame started the factory system; without cheap iron and coal steam engines could not be built and run. Judgement: It was the most transformative single invention, but it depended on earlier inventions and resources, and spread only gradually. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "The Industrial Revolution made life worse for most working people before 1850."
items.answer: Thesis: For many workers in the short term, yes – especially in health and conditions – though historians debate living standards and conditions improved later in the century.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: long hours, child labour and dangerous work in factories and mines; high death rates in overcrowded, insanitary towns. Counter-arguments: factory wages were often higher than farm wages; cheaper goods and, later, reforms improved some aspects of life. Thesis/conclusion: For many workers in the short term, yes – especially in health and conditions – though historians debate living standards and conditions improved later in the century. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. items.stem: "The benefits of industrialisation were shared fairly around the world." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Disagree: industrialisation brought wealth mainly to industrialised nations and their elites, while many colonies bore costs, creating a gap that still shapes development.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it eventually raised incomes and produced cheaper goods worldwide; railways and technology spread to many countries. Arguments against: colonies supplied raw materials and lost industries such as Indian textiles; industrial countries grew far richer, widening global inequality. Supported judgement: Disagree: industrialisation brought wealth mainly to industrialised nations and their elites, while many colonies bore costs, creating a gap that still shapes development. Markbands (12 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The change from hand production at home to machine production in factories, beginning in Britain from about 1760"?
items.answer: Industrial Revolution
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Industrial Revolution.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "spinning jenny".
items.answer: A multi-spindle spinning frame invented by James Hargreaves around 1764
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a multi-spindle spinning frame invented by James Hargreaves around 1764. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "public health"?
options: An overcrowded area of poor-quality housing without proper water supply or sanitation
The health of the population as a whole, protected by measures such as clean water, sewers and vaccination
Richard Arkwright's water-powered spinning machine (1769) that produced strong cotton thread
A method of production in which workers use powered machines in a central building under supervision and fixed hours
items.answer: The health of the population as a whole, protected by measures such as clean water, sewers and vaccination
items.markingKey: B. "public health" is the health of the population as a whole, protected by measures such as clean water, sewers and vaccination.

items.stem: A student claims: "Pollution from industry was only a problem in the 20th century." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Smog, polluted rivers and disease in industrial towns were already serious in the 19th century.
items.markingKey: Smog, polluted rivers and disease in industrial towns were already serious in the 19th century. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why Britain's geography helped it to industrialise first.
items.answer: It had large deposits of coal and iron near each other and near the coast, fast rivers for water power, many navigable rivers, and no place far from the sea for transport.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It had large deposits of coal and iron near each other and near the coast, fast rivers for water power, many navigable rivers, and no place far from the sea for transport. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between steam power and water power.
items.answer: Water power used water wheels and needed sites by fast rivers, limited by seasons; steam power burned coal, could be used anywhere coal was available, and produced more reliable power.
items.markingKey: Water power used water wheels and needed sites by fast rivers, limited by seasons; steam power burned coal, could be used anywhere coal was available, and produced more reliable power. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Industrial cities had high death rates because people were careless." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The causes were structural: overcrowding, no clean water, no sewers and low wages.
items.markingKey: The causes were structural: overcrowding, no clean water, no sewers and low wages. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between an industrialised economy and a colonial economy.
items.answer: An industrialised economy produces manufactured goods with machines; a colonial economy was often shaped to export raw materials to the colonial power and import its manufactures.
items.markingKey: An industrialised economy produces manufactured goods with machines; a colonial economy was often shaped to export raw materials to the colonial power and import its manufactures. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Britain industrialised first only because of clever inventors." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Inventions mattered, but so did coal, capital, markets, transport, agriculture, government and empire.
items.markingKey: Inventions mattered, but so did coal, capital, markets, transport, agriculture, government and empire. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830) and explain what it reveals about the impact of steam transport.
items.answer: It linked the port of Liverpool with the cotton mills of Manchester and carried passengers and freight by steam locomotive. Faster, cheaper links between port and mills cut costs and showed the commercial potential of railways.
items.markingKey: Context (It linked the port of Liverpool with the cotton mills of Manchester and carried passengers and freight by steam locomotive.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: faster, cheaper links between port and mills cut costs and showed the commercial potential of railways. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the impact of steam transport.

items.stem: Explain why "How far did the 1833 Factory Act improve the lives of child workers in Lancashire cotton mills by 1847?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into working and living conditions during industrialisation.
items.answer: It evaluates the impact of a specific reform using inspectors' reports and testimony.

The engineer told the committee that a train could carry passengers between Liverpool and Manchester in under two hours, compared with about four hours by coach, and could carry heavy goods such as cotton at a lower cost than the canal.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into the inventions of the Industrial Revolution and the factory system, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of evidence given to a Parliamentary committee on the Liverpool and Manchester Railway Bill, 1825. Purpose: to persuade MPs to approve the building of the railway. Value: It shows the arguments used by railway promoters and expected time and cost savings. Limitation: Promoters wanted the bill passed, so they may have exaggerated benefits; the canal owners opposed it.

items.stem:
Source A – Book on social conditions (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Friedrich Engels, "The Condition of the Working Class in England", 1845

The writer described a district of Manchester near the river where hundreds of families lived in cramped, damp cottages and cellars. There was a single privy for many people, filth lay in the courts, and the river was polluted by refuse from tanneries and dye works.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about working and living conditions during industrialisation. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Friedrich Engels, "The Condition of the Working Class in England", 1845. Purpose: to expose the conditions of industrial workers and criticise capitalism. Value: Engels observed Manchester first-hand over two years, giving detailed description of living conditions. Limitation: He was a socialist who wanted to show the evils of capitalism, so he may have chosen the worst districts; he wrote for a German audience.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Coal was the most important cause of the Industrial Revolution in Britain."
items.answer: Coal was essential for the later stages, but the revolution began through a combination of capital, markets, agriculture and invention.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it powered steam engines and smelted iron; Britain had large, accessible deposits. Arguments against: without capital, markets and inventions coal would have stayed underground; early factories used water power, not coal. Supported judgement: Coal was essential for the later stages, but the revolution began through a combination of capital, markets, agriculture and invention.
